notes.front: What is a team maintainer?
notes.back: A team member given the team-level team maintainer role, which grants a number of administrative permissions over that team.
notes.explanation: Team-level roles exist to give permissions to manage a team, and any individual member of a team can be given this one.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “About roles”
notes.evidence: Team-level roles are roles that give permissions to manage a team. You can give any individual member of a team the team maintainer role, which gives the member a number of administrative permissions over a team.
notes.example: Like a club member asked to keep one committee’s list of members in order, but with no say over the rest of the club.

notes.front: What is an organisation moderator?
notes.back: An organisation member who may also block and unblock non-member contributors, set interaction limits and hide comments in the organisation’s public repositories.
notes.explanation: These moderation powers come in addition to the person’s ordinary member permissions, not in place of them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Organization moderators”
notes.evidence: Moderators are organization members who, in addition to their permissions as members, are allowed to block and unblock non-member contributors, set interaction limits, and hide comments in public repositories owned by the organization.
notes.example: Like a volunteer on a public forum who can hide abusive posts and block troublemakers, but who otherwise posts as an ordinary user.

notes.front: What is an organisation billing manager?
notes.back: A user who can manage the organisation’s billing settings, such as payment information.
notes.explanation: The docs call it useful when the organisation’s members don’t usually have access to billing resources.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Billing managers”
notes.evidence: Billing managers are users who can manage the billing settings for your organization, such as payment information. This is a useful option if members of your organization don't usually have access to billing resources.
notes.example: Like a finance clerk trusted with the company card details, but not with the source code.

notes.front: What is the security manager role in an organisation?
notes.back: An organisation-level role to view security alerts and manage security feature settings across the organisation, with read permission for all its repositories.
notes.explanation: Organisation owners can assign it to any member or team in the organisation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Security managers”
notes.evidence: The security manager role is an organization-level role that organization owners can assign to any member or team in the organization. When applied, it gives permission to view security alerts and manage settings for security features across your organization, as well as read permission for all repositories in the organization.
notes.example: Like an inspector with a pass to read every building’s safety records and adjust its alarms, but not to rebuild anything.

notes.front: What is a GitHub App manager in an organisation?
notes.back: A user or team whom an organisation owner allows to manage the settings of some or all GitHub App registrations the organisation owns.
notes.explanation: By default only organisation owners can manage those settings; the role extends that to other users or teams.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “GitHub App managers”
notes.evidence: By default, only organization owners can manage the settings of GitHub App registrations owned by an organization. To allow additional users or teams to manage GitHub App registrations owned by an organization, an owner can grant them GitHub App manager permissions.
notes.example: Like a caretaker who may adjust the settings of the office’s delivery robots, but who is not the office owner.

notes.front: What is an enterprise owner?
notes.back: The enterprise role with complete control over the enterprise: it can take every action there.
notes.explanation: Its listed actions include managing administrators and adding and removing organisations.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Enterprise owners”
notes.evidence: Enterprise owners have complete control over the enterprise and can take every action, including: * Managing administrators * Adding and removing organizations
notes.example: Like the owner of a holding company who can open and close subsidiaries, but who is not automatically on each subsidiary’s staff.

notes.front: What is an unaffiliated user in an enterprise?
notes.back: A user who is not a member of any organisation and holds neither the enterprise owner nor the billing manager role.
notes.explanation: This is the label the enterprise uses for a user who belongs to the enterprise but to none of its organisations.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Unaffiliated users”
notes.evidence: If a user is not a member of any organization, and doesn't have the enterprise owner or billing manager role, the user is listed as an unaffiliated user.
notes.example: Like a card-holder of a library network who is not registered at any branch.

notes.front: What are an organisation’s base permissions?
notes.back: The permission level that applies to all organisation members when they access any of the organisation’s repositories.
notes.explanation: Because they apply to every member and every repository at once, one setting shapes access across the whole organisation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Setting base permissions for an organization”, “About base permissions for an organization”
notes.evidence: You can set base permissions that apply to all members of an organization when accessing any of the organization's repositories.
notes.example: Like a building’s default door pass that lets every employee into the shared floors, before anyone gets a key to a particular room.

notes.front: What is a custom repository role?
notes.back: A configurable set of repository permissions with a custom name you choose.
notes.explanation: It gives more granular control over the permissions you grant at repository level than the predefined roles alone.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About custom repository roles”, “About custom repository roles”
notes.evidence: You can have more granular control over the permissions you grant at the repository level by creating up to 20 custom repository roles. On GitHub Enterprise Server earlier than 3.19, you can create up to five custom repository roles. A custom repository role is a configurable set of permissions with a custom name you choose.
notes.example: Like the predefined Triage role, but renamed “Docs reviewer” and given one extra permission, such as managing wiki settings.

notes.front: In a custom repository role, what is the inherited role?
notes.back: The predefined role you start from when creating the custom role; it sets the role’s initial permissions.
notes.explanation: You then customise the role further by choosing additional permissions on top of the inherited ones.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About custom repository roles”, “About the inherited role”
notes.evidence: When you create a custom repository role, you start by choosing an inherited role from a set of pre-defined options. The inherited role determines the initial set of permissions included in the custom role. Then, you can further customize the role by choosing additional permissions to give the role.
notes.example: Like starting a new job description from the standard “editor” template, then adding one duty to it.

notes.front: What is a custom enterprise role?
notes.back: A role you define that grants access to a subset of enterprise settings, such as creating organisations.
notes.explanation: The feature is in public preview, and GitHub plans to add more permissions to choose from over time.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating custom roles in an enterprise”, “Creating enterprise custom roles”
notes.evidence: This feature is in public preview and subject to change. Enterprise custom roles grant access to a subset of enterprise settings, such as viewing audit logs and creating organizations. GitHub plans to expand the list of available permissions over time.
notes.example: Like giving a platform lead a key to the “create organisation” room of the enterprise, without handing over the whole building.

notes.front: What is an enterprise team?
notes.back: A team created in the enterprise to simplify administration at scale; for example, it can receive Copilot Business licences directly from the enterprise.
notes.explanation: Handling people as one enterprise-wide group, rather than organisation by organisation, is what makes administration at scale simpler.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating enterprise teams”, “Creating enterprise teams”
notes.evidence: To simplify administration at scale, you can create enterprise teams. Enterprise teams can: * Receive Copilot Business licenses directly from the enterprise.
notes.example: Like a company-wide mailing group that also carries software licences, rather than a group inside one department.

notes.front: Which level of role gives organisation members, outside collaborators and teams varying levels of access to repositories?
notes.back: Repository-level roles.
notes.explanation: The same repository roles can go to members, to outside collaborators or to whole teams.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “About roles”
notes.evidence: Repository-level roles give organization members, outside collaborators and teams of people varying levels of access to repositories.

notes.front: Which level of role can be assigned to individuals or teams to manage the organisation and its repositories, teams and settings?
notes.back: Organisation-level roles.
notes.explanation: These roles reach the organisation itself, not just one repository or one team.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “About roles”
notes.evidence: Organization-level roles are sets of permissions that can be assigned to individuals or teams to manage an organization and the organization's repositories, teams, and settings.

notes.front: The organisation owner role should be limited, but to no fewer than {{c1::two}} people.
notes.explanation: Owners have complete administrative access, so the docs ask for few of them, yet never just one.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Organization owners”
notes.evidence: Organization owners have complete administrative access to your organization. This role should be limited, but to no less than two people, in your organization.

notes.front: What access do organisation owners have to the organisation’s repositories?
notes.back: Admin access to every repository the organisation owns.
notes.explanation: This comes on top of managing organisation-level settings.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”
notes.evidence: In addition to managing organization-level settings, organization owners have admin access to every repository owned by the organization.

notes.front: Why do the docs suggest the security manager role for an organisation’s security team?
notes.back: It gives the team’s members the least access they need to the organisation.
notes.explanation: The role is suggested for exactly this case: a security team that needs work across the organisation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Security managers”
notes.evidence: If your organization has a security team, you can use the security manager role to give members of the team the least access they need to the organization.

notes.front: Does the GitHub App manager role let someone install or uninstall GitHub Apps on the organisation?
notes.back: No. It grants no access to install or uninstall GitHub Apps.
notes.explanation: The role covers managing the settings of App registrations, which is a different task from installing an app.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “GitHub App managers”
notes.evidence: The GitHub App manager role does not grant users access to install and uninstall GitHub Apps on an organization.

notes.front: Besides managing administrators and adding or removing organisations, what are two actions the docs list for enterprise owners?
notes.back: Any two, such as removing members from all organisations, enforcing policy across organisations, or managing billing or security settings.
notes.explanation: The list shows the role’s reach across every organisation in the enterprise at once.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Enterprise owners”
notes.evidence: Removing enterprise members from all organizations * Managing enterprise settings * Enforcing policy across organizations * Managing billing settings * Managing security settings

notes.front: Do enterprise owners have access to organisation settings or content by default?
notes.back: No, but they can gain access by joining any organisation.
notes.explanation: Control over the enterprise is not the same as membership of each organisation it owns.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Enterprise owners”
notes.evidence: Enterprise owners do not have access to organization settings or content by default, but they can gain access by joining any organization.

notes.front: Which organisation settings or content can an enterprise billing manager reach by default?
notes.back: None, except internal repositories within an enterprise in which they are a member.
notes.explanation: Their membership is what opens those internal repositories to them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Billing managers”
notes.evidence: Billing managers do not have access to organization settings or content by default except for internal repositories within an enterprise in which they are a member.

notes.front: What can an enterprise’s GitHub App managers do with the GitHub App registrations the enterprise owns?
notes.back: View, create, edit and delete them; they still cannot install or uninstall GitHub Apps.
notes.explanation: The same limit on installing applies at enterprise level as in an organisation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “App managers”
notes.evidence: Can view, create, edit, and delete GitHub App registrations that are owned by the enterprise. For the specific app settings that GitHub App managers can control, see Modifying a GitHub App registration. * Cannot install and uninstall GitHub Apps on an enterprise or organization.

notes.front: The enterprise security manager role is in {{c1::public preview}} and subject to change.
notes.explanation: Preview features can change without notice, so check the current GitHub Docs before relying on the role’s exact permissions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Security managers”
notes.evidence: The enterprise security manager role is in public preview and subject to change.

notes.front: Beyond their own organisations, which repositories can an enterprise’s organisation members access?
notes.back: All repositories with internal visibility in any organisation in the enterprise.
notes.explanation: Membership of one organisation opens internal repositories enterprise-wide.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Organization members”
notes.evidence: In addition to their access to organizations where they are members, these users can access all repositories with "internal" visibility in any organization in the enterprise.

notes.front: Can an unaffiliated user access the enterprise’s private or internal repositories?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The docs list this among the limits of the role, next to not consuming a licence unless another criterion applies.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Unaffiliated users”
notes.evidence: Do not consume a GitHub Enterprise license, unless they meet another criterion listed in People who consume a license in an organization. * Cannot access private or internal repositories.

notes.front: Do an organisation’s base permissions apply to outside collaborators?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The setting is defined for the organisation’s members, a group that outside collaborators are not part of.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Setting base permissions for an organization”, “About base permissions for an organization”
notes.evidence: You can set base permissions that apply to all members of an organization when accessing any of the organization's repositories. Base permissions do not apply to outside collaborators.

notes.front: By default, what permission do organisation members have on the organisation’s public repositories?
notes.back: Read.
notes.explanation: This is the level members get unless something else is set.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Setting base permissions for an organization”, “About base permissions for an organization”
notes.evidence: By default, members of an organization will have Read permissions to the organization's public repositories.

notes.front: A repository admin grants a member more access to one repository than the base permission gives. Which applies?
notes.back: The higher level of access overrides the base permission.
notes.explanation: Base permissions set a level for all members, but a higher grant on a repository wins there.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Setting base permissions for an organization”, “About base permissions for an organization”
notes.evidence: If someone with admin access to an organization's repository grants a member a higher level of access for the repository, the higher level of access overrides the base permission.

notes.front: If an organisation’s base permission is set to none, what minimum access do members keep to internal repositories?
notes.back: Read.
notes.explanation: Internal repositories keep a minimum visibility level of read whatever the base permission says.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Setting base permissions for an organization”, “About base permissions for an organization”
notes.evidence: Internal repositories have a minimum visibility level of read, even if the base permission has been set to none.

notes.front: Which organisations can create custom repository roles?
notes.back: Only organisations that use GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
notes.explanation: The note on the page restricts the feature to that product.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About custom repository roles”, “About custom repository roles”
notes.evidence: Only organizations that use GitHub Enterprise Cloud can create custom repository roles.

notes.front: An organisation can create up to {{c1::20}} custom repository roles.
notes.explanation: On GitHub Enterprise Server earlier than 3.19 the limit is five.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About custom repository roles”, “About custom repository roles”
notes.evidence: creating up to 20 custom repository roles. On GitHub Enterprise Server earlier than 3.19, you can create up to five custom repository roles.

notes.front: Which inherited role is designed for non-code contributors who want to view or discuss your project?
notes.back: Read.
notes.explanation: Its description matches people who only view or discuss the project.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About custom repository roles”, “About the inherited role”
notes.evidence: Non-code contributors who want to view or discuss your project

notes.front: Which inherited role is designed for contributors who need to proactively manage issues and pull requests without write access?
notes.back: Triage.
notes.explanation: This is the Triage role you already know; choosing it as the inherited role gives the custom role Triage’s permissions as its starting set, before you add more.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About custom repository roles”, “About the inherited role”
notes.evidence: Contributors who need to proactively manage issues and pull requests without write access

notes.front: Which inherited role is designed for organisation members and collaborators who actively push to your project?
notes.back: Write.
notes.explanation: Its description centres on actively pushing to the project.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About custom repository roles”, “About the inherited role”
notes.evidence: Organization members and collaborators who actively push to your project

notes.front: Which inherited role is designed for project managers who need to manage the repository without access to sensitive or destructive actions?
notes.back: Maintain.
notes.explanation: This is the Maintain role you already know; choosing it as the inherited role gives the custom role Maintain’s permissions as its starting set, before you add more.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About custom repository roles”, “About the inherited role”
notes.evidence: Project managers who need to manage the repository without access to sensitive or destructive actions

notes.front: Someone gets access to a repository through several avenues, such as team membership and base permissions. What access do they end up with?
notes.back: The sum of all the access grants: roles and permissions are additive.
notes.explanation: No single avenue cancels another; each adds to the total.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About custom repository roles”, “Precedence for different levels of access”
notes.evidence: Roles and permissions are additive. If a person is given different levels of access through different avenues, such as team membership and the base permissions for an organization, the user has the sum of all access grants.

notes.front: Can enterprise owners assign the custom organisation roles they create at enterprise level?
notes.back: No. They can create and edit them; organisation owners assign them.
notes.explanation: The enterprise defines the role once, and each organisation decides who holds it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating custom roles in an enterprise”, “Creating organization custom roles”
notes.evidence: Enterprise owners can create and edit custom organization roles, but cannot assign them. Organization owners can assign custom roles in an organization.

notes.front: An enterprise can create up to {{c1::20}} custom organisation roles, and each organisation can also create up to 20.
notes.explanation: The enterprise’s limit is separate from each organisation’s own.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating custom roles in an enterprise”, “Creating organization custom roles”
notes.evidence: An enterprise can create up to 20 custom organization roles. This limit applies to the enterprise: each organization can also create up to 20 custom organization roles.

notes.front: What happens when you remove a user from an enterprise team?
notes.back: They lose the privileges associated with the team, but stay in the enterprise account.
notes.explanation: Team membership carries privileges; it is not what makes someone part of the enterprise.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating enterprise teams”, “Creating enterprise teams”
notes.evidence: Removing a user from a team removes those privileges, but does not remove the user from the enterprise account.

notes.front: Which roles can an enterprise team be assigned, giving its members access to enterprise settings?
notes.back: Predefined and custom enterprise roles.
notes.explanation: The role then gives the team’s members access to enterprise settings.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating enterprise teams”, “Creating enterprise teams”
notes.evidence: Be assigned **predefined and custom enterprise roles**, giving members access to enterprise settings.

notes.front: When you give an enterprise team access to an organisation, how are its members added?
notes.back: Directly, without an invitation, with the same access as other organisation members.
notes.explanation: No invitation step stands between the team’s organisation access and membership.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating enterprise teams”, “2. Create a team”
notes.evidence: When you give a team access to organizations, members of the team are added directly to those organizations, without an invitation, and receive the same access as other organization members.

notes.front: An enterprise team with organisation access contains outside collaborators and unaffiliated users. What happens to them?
notes.back: They become standard enterprise members, with access to internal repositories, and consume a GitHub Enterprise licence.
notes.explanation: Organisation access through the team turns them into members like any other.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating enterprise teams”, “2. Create a team”
notes.evidence: Outside collaborators and unaffiliated users in the team become standard enterprise members, meaning they have access to your enterprise's internal repositories and consume a GitHub Enterprise license.

notes.front: Organisation administrators can give an enterprise team more access, but {{c1::cannot remove}} any permissions granted by enterprise administrators.
notes.explanation: What the enterprise grants, the organisation can add to but not take away.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating enterprise teams”, “2. Create a team”
notes.evidence: Organization administrators can give the team additional repository access and assign them organization-level roles, but cannot remove any permissions granted by enterprise administrators.

notes.front: What are the limits on enterprise teams?
notes.back: Up to 2,500 teams per enterprise, 5,000 users per team, and 1,000 organisations per team.
notes.explanation: The limits apply per enterprise, per team, and to each team’s organisations respectively.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating enterprise teams”, “Creating enterprise teams”
notes.evidence: You can create up to 2,500 teams for a single enterprise and add up to 5,000 users to each team. Each team can be assigned to a maximum of 1,000 organizations.

notes.front: Which enterprises can sync an enterprise team’s membership to a group in their identity provider?
notes.back: Only those that use Enterprise Managed Users.
notes.explanation: Changes made to the group in the identity provider, such as adding or removing a user, are then synced to the team.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating enterprise teams”, “Syncing with an IdP group”
notes.evidence: If you use Enterprise Managed Users, you can sync membership of an enterprise team to a group in your identity provider. That way, any changes made to the group in the IdP (such as adding or removing a user) will be synced to the enterprise team

notes.front: What happens if the IdP group synced to an enterprise team grows beyond 5,000 users?
notes.back: The team stops being synced.
notes.explanation: The 5,000 figure is the enterprise team size limit itself.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating enterprise teams”, “Limits on IdP group sizes”
notes.evidence: If an IdP group goes over the team size limit of 5,000 users, the team will stop being synced.

notes.front: On the enterprise’s Members page, why can the “total consumed” licence figure exceed the number of people listed?
notes.back: Outside collaborators consume a licence but are not counted in the member total.
notes.explanation: Pending invitations to outside collaborators also consume a licence without appearing in the invitation count.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Viewing people in your enterprise”, “User licenses consumed”
notes.evidence: An outside collaborator consumes a license, but is not counted in the total member count displayed next to "people in YOUR-ENTERPRISE". A pending invitation to an outside collaborator also consumes a license, but is not counted in the "By invitations" count in the overview.

notes.front: How does the overview on an enterprise’s Members page group members?
notes.back: By role, type of licence consumed, and type of deployment.
notes.explanation: The three groupings are role, licence consumed and deployment.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Viewing people in your enterprise”, “About the membership overview”
notes.evidence: you will find an overview of the number of members in your enterprise, grouped by role, type of license consumed, and the type of deployment the member is on.

notes.front: What are two things the enterprise membership information report records about each user?
notes.back: Two of: username and display name; whether two-factor authentication is enabled and how secure it is; organisation owner or member status.
notes.explanation: The report covers everyone associated with the enterprise, whether or not they consume a licence.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Exporting membership information for your enterprise”, “About export of membership information”
notes.evidence: Username and display name details * Whether the user has two-factor authentication enabled and how secure their 2FA configuration is * Whether the user is an organization owner or member

notes.front: What are two uses the docs give for the list of people with access to a repository?
notes.back: Two of: helping off-board people, gathering data for compliance, and general security checkups.
notes.explanation: The same list supports both people management and compliance work.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Viewing people with access to your repository”, “About the list of people with access to your repository”
notes.evidence: You can use this information to help off-board people, gather data for compliance, and other general security checkups.

notes.front: Which repository role is needed to enable the dependency graph for a private repository?
notes.back: Admin.
notes.explanation: The access table ticks only the Admin column for this action.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Access requirements for security features”
notes.evidence: Enable the dependency graph for a private repository | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓

notes.front: Your organisation has one owner, who is about to go on long leave. Following GitHub’s guidance on the owner role, what should you do?
notes.back: D: add at least one more owner, keeping the role limited.
notes.explanation: The docs say the owner role should be limited, but to no fewer than two people.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Organization owners”
notes.evidence: Organization owners have complete administrative access to your organization. This role should be limited, but to no less than two people, in your organization.
notes.choices:
A) Make every member an owner so someone can always act
B) Leave it: one owner is the recommended number
C) Rely on a moderator to cover owner duties
D) Add at least one more owner, keeping the role limited
notes.choicesExplained: A: the role should be limited, and owners have complete administrative access. C: moderators only add moderation powers to member permissions. B: the guidance asks for no fewer than two owners.

notes.front: A finance colleague must update the organisation’s payment information. They do not work on code. Which role fits?
notes.back: C: billing manager.
notes.explanation: Billing managers can manage the organisation’s billing settings, such as payment information.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Billing managers”
notes.evidence: Billing managers are users who can manage the billing settings for your organization, such as payment information.
notes.choices:
A) Security manager
B) Moderator
C) Billing manager
D) Team maintainer
notes.choicesExplained: A: the security manager role is for security alerts and settings, with read access to repositories. B: moderators block contributors, set interaction limits and hide comments. D: a team maintainer manages a team.

notes.front: Your security team must view security alerts and manage security feature settings across every repository in the organisation, with the least access that does this. What do you give the team?
notes.back: D: the security manager role.
notes.explanation: The docs suggest this role to give a security team the least access they need to the organisation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Security managers”
notes.evidence: If your organization has a security team, you can use the security manager role to give members of the team the least access they need to the organization.
notes.choices:
A) Organisation owner
B) GitHub App manager
C) Maintain on each repository
D) The security manager role
notes.choicesExplained: A: owners have complete administrative access, far more than needed. B: that role manages GitHub App registrations. C: a repository role must be granted repository by repository and is not the role the docs suggest for this.

notes.front: A developer was made GitHub App manager for all the organisation’s App registrations. They now cannot install one of the apps on the organisation. Why?
notes.back: D: the role does not grant access to install or uninstall GitHub Apps.
notes.explanation: The role covers managing the settings of App registrations, not installing apps.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “GitHub App managers”
notes.evidence: The GitHub App manager role does not grant users access to install and uninstall GitHub Apps on an organization.
notes.choices:
A) App managers must first be made moderators
B) They were given only some of the registrations
C) Only enterprise owners can hold the GitHub App manager role
D) The GitHub App manager role does not grant access to install or uninstall GitHub Apps
notes.choicesExplained: B: they manage all the registrations, and even full scope would not include installing. C: an organisation owner grants the role to users or teams. A: moderation has nothing to do with GitHub Apps.

notes.front: A newly appointed enterprise owner opens one of the enterprise’s organisations and cannot see its settings or repositories. What explains this, and what can they do?
notes.back: A: enterprise owners have no organisation access by default, but can join any organisation.
notes.explanation: Complete control of the enterprise does not by default include organisation settings or content.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Enterprise owners”
notes.evidence: Enterprise owners do not have access to organization settings or content by default, but they can gain access by joining any organization.
notes.choices:
A) Enterprise owners lack organisation access by default; they can join the organisation
B) They need the billing manager role as well
C) Their account is broken; they should contact support
D) They must create a custom repository role first
notes.choicesExplained: C: this is the expected default, not a fault. B: enterprise billing managers do not have organisation access by default either. D: a custom repository role controls repository permissions and is assigned by repository admins.

notes.front: An enterprise billing manager, who is not an owner, wants to know which organisation content they can see by default. What is the answer?
notes.back: D: only internal repositories within an enterprise in which they are a member.
notes.explanation: Organisation settings and content are closed to the role by default, with that one exception.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Billing managers”
notes.evidence: Billing managers do not have access to organization settings or content by default except for internal repositories within an enterprise in which they are a member.
notes.choices:
A) All organisation settings in the enterprise
B) Every organisation’s security alerts
C) Every private repository in the enterprise
D) Only internal repositories within an enterprise in which they are a member
notes.choicesExplained: A: billing managers do not have access to organisation settings by default. C: private repositories are not included. B: security alerts belong to security roles, not billing.

notes.front: A user belongs to no organisation, holds no enterprise role, and sits in an enterprise team that has a Copilot licence but no organisation access. They try to open an internal repository. What happens?
notes.back: C: they cannot; unaffiliated users cannot access private or internal repositories.
notes.explanation: Without organisation membership they are an unaffiliated user, whatever their team or licence.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Unaffiliated users”
notes.evidence: Cannot access private or internal repositories. * Can be added as members of enterprise teams. * Can receive a Copilot license or custom role directly from your enterprise.
notes.choices:
A) They can open it, because enterprise team members see all internal repositories
B) They can open it read-only, because internal repositories keep read access
C) They cannot: unaffiliated users cannot access private or internal repositories
D) They can open it once their Copilot licence is active
notes.choicesExplained: A: enterprise team membership alone does not give organisation membership here, as the team has no organisation access. B: the minimum read on internal repositories applies to organisation members. D: a Copilot licence does not grant repository access.

notes.front: In an enterprise with managed users, a contractor is provisioned as a guest collaborator and added as a member of one organisation, “Payments”. Which internal repositories can they access?
notes.back: A: only the internal repositories of the Payments organisation.
notes.explanation: Guest collaborators cannot access internal repositories except in organisations where they are added as a member.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Guest collaborators”
notes.evidence: Cannot access internal repositories in the enterprise, except in organizations where they're added as a member. The difference between a guest collaborator and a regular user is that when a regular user is added to one organization, they can automatically access all internal repositories in the enterprise.
notes.choices:
A) Only the internal repositories of the Payments organisation
B) All internal repositories in the enterprise
C) None, because guest collaborators cannot join organisations
D) Only repositories where they are an outside collaborator
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is what a regular user gets when added to one organisation. C: guest collaborators can be added as organisation members. D: they are a member of Payments, not a repository-by-repository collaborator, and membership opens Payments’ internal repositories.

notes.front: An organisation owner sets base permissions to none. A member has no team or individual grants on an internal repository in that organisation. What access do they have to it?
notes.back: C: read.
notes.explanation: Internal repositories have a minimum visibility level of read, even when base permissions are none.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Setting base permissions for an organization”, “About base permissions for an organization”
notes.evidence: Internal repositories have a minimum visibility level of read, even if the base permission has been set to none.
notes.choices:
A) None
B) Write
C) Read
D) Triage
notes.choicesExplained: A: none applies to private repositories without other grants, not internal ones. B: write would need a higher grant or base permission. D: triage is not given by the internal minimum.

notes.front: An organisation raises its base permissions from Read to Write. A consultant who is an outside collaborator on one repository asks whether their access has changed. What do you tell them?
notes.back: B: nothing changes; base permissions do not apply to outside collaborators.
notes.explanation: Base permissions apply to all members of the organisation, and an outside collaborator is not a member.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Setting base permissions for an organization”, “About base permissions for an organization”
notes.evidence: You can set base permissions that apply to all members of an organization when accessing any of the organization's repositories. Base permissions do not apply to outside collaborators.
notes.choices:
A) They now have Write on every repository
B) Nothing changes: base permissions do not apply to outside collaborators
C) They now have Write on their one repository
D) They lose access until re-invited
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: both assume base permissions reach outside collaborators, which they do not. D: changing base permissions does not remove anyone’s access.

notes.front: In an organisation on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, technical writers on one documentation repository should view and discuss it and also manage its wiki settings, without pushing code. What do you set up?
notes.back: C: a custom repository role inheriting Read, plus “Manage wiki settings”.
notes.explanation: A custom repository role starts from an inherited role and can then be given additional permissions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About custom repository roles”, “About the inherited role”
notes.evidence: When you create a custom repository role, you start by choosing an inherited role from a set of pre-defined options. The inherited role determines the initial set of permissions included in the custom role. Then, you can further customize the role by choosing additional permissions to give the role.
notes.choices:
A) A custom organisation role, since it covers all current and future repositories
B) Raise base permissions to Maintain
C) A custom repository role inheriting Read, plus “Manage wiki settings”
D) A custom repository role inheriting Admin, minus destructive actions
notes.choicesExplained: A: a custom organisation role reaches all repositories, not one. B: base permissions would change access for every member on every repository. D: Admin is not one of the inherited role options (Read, Triage, Write, Maintain).

notes.front: An organisation on GitHub Enterprise Server 3.18 already has five custom repository roles and wants a sixth. What is the position?
notes.back: A: it has reached the limit; before 3.19 the limit is five.
notes.explanation: The limit of 20 applies elsewhere; GitHub Enterprise Server earlier than 3.19 allows five.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About custom repository roles”, “About custom repository roles”
notes.evidence: creating up to 20 custom repository roles. On GitHub Enterprise Server earlier than 3.19, you can create up to five custom repository roles.
notes.choices:
A) It has reached the limit: before 3.19 the limit is five
B) It can create up to 20, so a sixth is fine
C) Custom repository roles are not available on GitHub Enterprise Server at all
D) It can create a sixth only as an inherited role
notes.choicesExplained: B: 20 is not the limit for versions earlier than 3.19. C: the docs give a limit for GitHub Enterprise Server, so the feature exists there. D: an inherited role is only the starting point of a custom role, not a separate kind of role.

notes.front: A member holds a custom repository role based on Read, with one extra permission, on a repository. Their team is then given Write on the same repository. What access do they have?
notes.back: B: Write, plus the custom role’s extra permission.
notes.explanation: Roles and permissions are additive, so the person has the sum of all access grants.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About custom repository roles”, “Precedence for different levels of access”
notes.evidence: Roles and permissions are additive. If a person is given different levels of access through different avenues, such as team membership and the base permissions for an organization, the user has the sum of all access grants.
notes.choices:
A) Read plus the extra permission, since the custom role takes priority
B) Write, plus the custom role’s extra permission
C) Write only; the custom role is cancelled
D) A conflict that blocks access until resolved
notes.choicesExplained: A: no grant takes priority to reduce access. C: nothing is cancelled; grants add up. D: conflicting access shows a warning but is not blocked.

notes.front: You want to give Copilot Business licences to 300 people spread over twelve organisations, managed as one group at enterprise level. What do you use?
notes.back: B: an enterprise team.
notes.explanation: Enterprise teams exist to simplify administration at scale and can receive Copilot Business licences directly from the enterprise.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating enterprise teams”, “Creating enterprise teams”
notes.evidence: To simplify administration at scale, you can create enterprise teams. Enterprise teams can: * Receive Copilot Business licenses directly from the enterprise.
notes.choices:
A) A nested team in each organisation
B) An enterprise team
C) A custom repository role
D) Outside collaborator invitations
notes.choicesExplained: A: nested teams live inside a single organisation. C: a custom repository role sets repository permissions, not licences. D: outside collaborators are given repository access, not licences.

notes.front: An auditor sees more licences consumed than people listed on the enterprise’s Members page. Several contractors work only as outside collaborators. Which explanation fits?
notes.back: B: outside collaborators consume a licence but are not counted in the member total.
notes.explanation: The docs name this as why “total consumed” may exceed the number of people listed.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Viewing people in your enterprise”, “User licenses consumed”
notes.evidence: If there are outside collaborators in your enterprise, the "total consumed" number of licenses may be larger than the number of people listed for your enterprise.
notes.choices:
A) Unaffiliated users always consume a licence
B) Outside collaborators consume a licence but are not in the member total
C) Enterprise owners consume two licences each
D) Each person is counted once per organisation
notes.choicesExplained: A: unaffiliated users do not consume a licence unless they meet another criterion. D: the per-role counting applies to the Roles column, not licences. C: the docs say nothing of the kind.

notes.front: Custom organisation role versus custom repository role: which repositories does each reach?
notes.back: A custom organisation role: all current and future repositories in the organisation. A custom repository role: specific repositories.
notes.explanation: Pick the organisation role for organisation-wide duties, and the repository role for access to particular repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About custom repository roles”, “About custom repository roles”
notes.evidence: Custom organization roles differ from repository roles by granting permissions across all current and future repositories in the organization. Custom repository roles, however, allow you to grant permissions to specific repositories within the organization.
